analysis.one_liner: Requires HHS to publicly name hospitals that fail to post their prices online.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2022 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals have been legally required since 2021 to post clear, accessible pricing for their services online. This bill would force the Health and Human Services Department to publish a public list of every hospital caught not complying — including any that got a penalty, a warning, or even a letter about possible violations — and to make those enforcement records fully public. It would also require annual reports to Congress on enforcement and a study on tougher consequences, including stripping tax-exempt status from hospitals that refuse to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary patients, employers who buy health coverage for workers, and anyone trying to compare hospital prices before getting care. Hospitals that don't comply with the existing price transparency rule could face public shaming, and the bill sets up a path toward bigger penalties and loss of tax-exempt status for repeat offenders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers shopping for care

how_it_helps.text: Requires CMS to maintain a public list of hospitals found out of compliance with the price transparency rule, including those that received a civil monetary penalty, a warning notice, a corrective action plan request, or any written notice of potential noncompliance.
Makes all penalties, notices, and enforcement communications subject to full public disclosure without redaction.

Requires the Secretary to report to Congress annually on complaints and enforcement activity, and requires a Government Accountability Office report with recommendations for improving transparency, revoking or suspending tax-exempt status for noncompliant hospitals, and increasing penalty amounts.
Requires the Secretary, within 180 days of the GAO report, to propose rules based on those recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, especially those hiding or obscuring their negotiated prices, would bear the cost of public identification, potential larger civil monetary penalties, and the risk of losing 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status. Patients would not pay anything directly, though hospitals could resist by spending more on compliance and lobbying.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself raise penalties or strip tax exemptions; it only publishes names and orders a study and a proposed rule, so actual consequences would arrive a year or more after enactment, if at all.

Publishing warning notices and corrective action requests in full, before a hospital has had a chance to contest them, could publicly brand hospitals as violators on the basis of preliminary enforcement steps rather than final adjudicated violations.

A fair objection from supporters of transparency is that the underlying price transparency rule already existed with civil monetary penalty authority, and enforcement had been slow — a list and reports do not guarantee faster enforcement.

The bill text contains a drafting error, citing the Freedom of Information Act disclosure provision under title 21 rather than title 5 of the U.S. Code, which courts would likely have had to sort out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea is cheap for the public and pointed at a real problem: the hospital price transparency rule exists, and enforcement had produced few penalties relative to widespread noncompliance. But the bill is an enforcement-visibility measure, not an enforcement-strength measure — it names names and orders studies rather than raising fines or revoking tax status directly. The strongest version of the bill would have bundled the penalty increases and tax-exempt consequences in as requirements, not merely recommendations for a later rulemaking.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in June 2022, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced S. 4414 on June 15, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party.
No further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — was ever taken on the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that were out of compliance with the price transparency rule are better off, because no public list of violators was ever created and the threat of larger penalties or tax-exempt consequences went nowhere. Patients and employers remain dependent on the existing, weakly enforced rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that never posted their prices

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration after it was referred to HELP; it received no markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and its sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would publicly identify hospitals that fail to post their negotiated prices, exposing them to reputational damage and paving the way for larger fines and possible loss of tax-exempt status. Many hospitals had quietly not complied with the 2021 transparency rule, and a public list would give patients and employers leverage they do not currently have.
The GAO report is explicitly required to address improving transparency for employers, who pay for care on behalf of workers and have been among the loudest demanders of hospital price data.
